Regression Continued

Controlled Regression

Remember

  • Coefficients represent the effect of a one-unit increase in the IV on the expected value of the DV. It’s important to pay attention to what a “one unit” change would mean in terms of the IV (Is it a percent? A dollar? A thousand dollars?) and the DV.

  • Each coefficient in a regression will have its own standard error and p.value. Some coefficients may be significant and others might not be.

  • When you include additional variables in a model, interpret the coefficient as the effect of a one unit change in X controlling for everything else in the model.

Reading a regression table

  • We’ll look at an example of a table of regressions that you might see in a published academic article and walk through how to interpret it.

  • Not all tables will be the same, but there are some conventions that are somewhat consistent across different outlets.

Reading a regression table

  • Regression table on the right comes from a 2006 paper by Daniel Kono titled Optimal Obfuscation: Democracy and Trade Policy Transparency Kono (2006)
  • Kono argues that democracy prompts states to reduce “transparent barriers” to trade but replace them with less transparent barriers.

Theoretical argument

Kono’s basic argument:

  • Politicians want votes and money.

  • Special interest groups want to be protected from trade, so having trade barriers is a way to get campaign donations.

  • Trade barriers make things more expensive, but voters don’t always know who to blame for high prices. This is especially true when the barriers and more complicated.

  • Politicians in democracies prefer non-tariff barriers (such as stringent quality controls, licenses, or quotas) because they can please special interests but voters don’t understand them.

Expectations

  • Countries that are more democratic will have lower tariffs.

  • Countries that are more democratic will have higher non-tariff barriers.

Using a model to test a hypothesis

So how do we get to this?

Using a model to test a hypothesis

  • Polity is a measure of democracy. Higher values = more democracy. This is our main IV.
  • Not all variables are included in all models. So you see blanks when those controls are omitted from one model.
  • This model contains a number of additional controls beyond the main IV. (note: ln means the natural log was taken, and \(\Delta\) means his variable is the change from a previous period.)
  • Asterisks are a common way to give a quick indication of statistical significance.

Using a model to test a hypothesis

  • Kono includes “electoral competition” as an alternative measure of his IV. If the theory is correct, you would expect it to apply more strongly in countries that had more electoral competition.

Using a model to test a hypothesis

Finally, we’ve got hypotheses about different dependent variables. So there are models for three different dependent variables.

Kono argued that tariffs would decrease as democracy increased, but non-tariff barriers (Core NTB and Quality NTB) would go up. Are these result consistent with this hypothesis?

Using a model to test a hypothesis

Predictions from a model

For now, we can work with a simpler model.

  • The dependent variable here is the Democratic percentage of the two party presidential vote in 2024.

  • Right now I have one predictor: median income.

  • What is the predicted value of the dependent variable when a state has a median income of $70,000?

Predictions from a model

Going back to our formula:

\[ \hat{y} = \alpha + \beta_1x_1 \]

\[ \text{Dem %} = 1.6 + 5.8 \times \text{Median income (\$10,000)} \]

\[ \text{Dem %} = 1.6 + 5.8 \times 7 = 42.2 \]

Predictions with a control

  • I’ll add a control variable for the % of the state population over the age of 25.

  • Notice the change in the intercept, as well as a small change in the coefficient for median income.

  • Now what is the predicted value of the DV when 70% of the population is over 25 and the median income is 70,000?

Predictions with a control

Going back to our formula:

\[ \hat{y} = \alpha + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2 \]

\[ \text{Dem %} = -120.4 + 5.1 \times \text{Median income (\$10,000)} + 1.8 \times \text{% over 25} \]

So now we plug in those values:

\[ \text{Dem %} = -120.4 + 5.1 \times 7 + 1.8 \times 70 = 41.3 \]

Predictions with a dummy variable

  • I’ve added variable that is equal to 1 if a states is in the northeast, and 0 otherwise.

  • How should I interpret this? It’s technically still the effect of a one-unit increase in the IV, but in this case there’s a more straightforward interpretation.

Predictions with a dummy variable

Back to the formula

\[ \hat{y} = \alpha + \beta_1x_1 \]

\[ \text{Dem %} = 44.5 + \text{Northeastern State} \times 11.9 \]

If we plug in a “1” here, we get the prediction for northeastern states.

\[ \text{Dem %} = 44.5 + 1 \times 11.9 = 56.4 \]

If we plug in a “0” here, we get the prediction for every other region

\[ \text{Dem %} = 44.5 + 0 \times 11.9 = 44.5 \]

Predictions with multiple dummies

What if I have a variable that takes on more than 2 categories? For example: what if I want to include all the regions of the US?

State Region
Alabama South
Maine Northeast
Ohio Midwest
Colorado West

We can handle this by making a dummy variable for all of the categories. These tables have the same info:

State South Northeast Midwest West
Alabama 1 0 0 0
Maine 0 1 0 0
Ohio 0 0 1 0
Colorado 0 0 0 1

Predictions with multiple dummies

regC(dem_percent ~ region, data=election)

R will actually do this “dummifying” process automatically when we include a categorical variable in a model. But you might notice something missing here.

But what happened to the Midwest?? Does R hate the heartland??

Predictions with multiple dummies

  • R has to drop one of the four categories to avoid what’s called the “dummy trap”

  • If we’re already accounting for “South”, “Northeast”, and “West”, then “Midwest” is always 1, so “a one unit change in X” never happens.

  • R chooses to drop the Midwest because it’s first alphabetically, but we have to drop something.

State South Northeast Midwest West
Ohio 0 0 1 0

Predictions with multiple dummies

  • Technically, the Midwest is still represented here, it’s just represented by the intercept term.

  • And all of the coefficients should be interpreted as being the difference between the excluded category (Midwest) and that dummy.

Predictions with multiple dummies

  • Think of the excluded category as the baseline.
  • And think of each coefficient as representing the difference between that category and the excluded group.

Predictions with multiple dummies

Going back to the equation for each prediction, we can think of our model as looking like this.

\[ \text{Dem %} = 43.6 + (\text{Northeast}\times 12.8) + (\text{South} \times -1.3) + (\text{West} \times 4.3) \]

So, if we want the prediction for the Northeast, we can get it by plugging in the values for each coefficient:

\(\text{Dem %} = 43.6 + (1\times 12.8) + (0 \times -1.3) + (0 \times 4.3)\)

Or, even more simply

\(\text{Dem %} = 43.6 + 12.8 = 56.4\)

Predictions with multiple dummies

\[ \text{Dem %} = 43.6 + (\text{Northeast}\times 12.8) + (\text{South} \times -1.3) + (\text{West} \times 4.3) \]

  • \(\text{Northeast %} = 43.6 + 12.8 = 56.4\)

  • \(\text{South %} = 43.6 -1.3 = 42.3\)

  • \(\text{West %} = 43.6 + 4.3 = 47.9\)

  • \(\text{Midwest %} = 43.6\)

Predictions with multiple dummies

  • Note that choosing to exclude a different group will change the coefficients AND the p-values. In essence, each p-value tells you whether that coefficient is different from the excluded group.

Predictions with multiple dummies

You can use the relevel function to change the category that’s automatically excluded from the regression results.

# Make the excluded category South
election$region<-relevel(election$region, ref="South")
regC(dem_percent ~ region, data=election)

Types of relationship

We talked about three general ways that more than two variables could be related in a controlled comparison.

  • Spurious: controlling for Z removes or reverses the effect of X on Y

  • Additive: Z and X impact Y independently

  • Interactive: the effect of X depends on values of Z

Model
